title: From Eyeballs to Annual Run Rates (ARR): Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the Anthropic Trade!
gist: Damodaran argues young companies like Anthropic ($67B ARR, $965B May VC round) and OpenAI ($852B, pending ~$1.4T) are priced rather than valued because earnings and cash flows are negative, so revenue-run-rate, user or compute multiples dominate — but ARR is non-standard (OpenAI's net-revenue switch cut ARR from $70B to $50B), peers are scarce, and any multiple embeds implicit growth, margin and risk assumptions; he stays neutral until the prospectus supports an intrinsic valuation.

themes.theme: Anthropic and OpenAI facts as of October 2026

insights.claim: Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, described as up 45% from the prior quarter, with positive profit only on an adjusted basis, and an annual revenue run rate of $67 billion expected to exceed $100 billion by year-end, at a pre-IPO investor meeting on October 15.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Sets the reported growth base against which an IPO of $1.5T or more would be priced.
insights.locator: I was in San Francisco last week

insights.claim: Anthropic's May 2026 venture round raised $65 billion at a $965 billion post-money pricing, OpenAI raised $122 billion at an $852 billion post-money price in March 2026, and OpenAI has a pending pre-IPO raise of about $30 billion at roughly $1.4 trillion.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Private marks have run from under $1T to above $1.4T within months; IPO pricing anchors will start there.
insights.locator: Anthropic's VC round in May 2026

insights.claim: Both Anthropic and OpenAI are rumored to be considering IPOs at market capitalizations above a trillion dollars, and Damodaran frames them as young growth companies despite their scale because of sky-high growth, operating losses and negative free cash flow.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Scaled-but-young profile means standard mature-company screens do not apply.
insights.locator: How do Anthropic and OpenAI measure up in the life cycle?

insights.claim: Damodaran does not believe Anthropic's claim of profitability in the second quarter of 2026, because the profits are adjusted and the adjustments are a patchwork of add-backs of legitimate expenses.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Treat adjusted profitability claims skeptically in the S-1; look for GAAP and cash flow.
insights.locator: I know that Anthropic claimed to be profitable

insights.claim: Whether Anthropic and OpenAI, both deep in negative free cash flow, ever generate positive cash flows is entirely a function of how the AI business evolves, and their business models (usage versus subscription, premium versus mass market) are still in flux.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Cash-flow breakeven timing is the key underwriting uncertainty for AI lab valuation.
insights.locator: How do Anthropic and OpenAI measure up

insights.claim: Valuation estimates intrinsic value from cash flows, growth and risk, while pricing sets value from what others pay for similar assets, reducing it to demand and supply; if you believed price converges to value in efficient markets, you would simply buy index funds.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Clarifies that IPO-era AI debate is mostly about pricing mechanics, not value.
insights.locator: Pricing versus Valuation: Across the life cycle

insights.claim: Young companies have little in their financial statements, uncertain market size and no stable industry benchmarks, so valuing them is always more complicated, and most investors turn away from valuation and fall back to pricing.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Expect IPO debate to be dominated by comparables and narratives.
insights.locator: If you frame an intrinsic valuation

insights.claim: Venture capital pricing is almost always forward pricing: for Anthropic and OpenAI it is compressed and less informative because investors treat them as imminent IPOs and price off expected IPO pricing minus a discount for negative surprises.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Private-round valuations are not independent evidence of value; they are expectations of the IPO price.
insights.locator: While you may be tempted to assume that the VC pricing

insights.claim: At the time of Anthropic's May round the expected IPO pricing was $1.15 trillion, well below current expectations, so the $965 billion round price represented a $150 billion discount that illustrates how fast young-company expectations change.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Shows IPO price expectations rose sharply in five months, raising the bar for post-IPO performance.
insights.locator: For Anthropic, for instance, at the time of the VC round

insights.claim: Early in the corporate life cycle, with losses, negative cash flows and little tangible capital, revenue is often the only viable pricing metric: 'desperation drives you up the income statement until you find a positive number.'
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Revenue multiples will dominate AI lab comparisons until margins appear.
insights.quote: desperation drives you up the income statement until you find a positive number
insights.locator: 1. Pricing metrics

insights.claim: Annualized revenue run rate is not standardized and is easily gamed: it can be computed from the last day, week or month, and gross versus net revenue treatment changes it materially.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Compare ARR across companies only after normalizing for gross/net and annualization period.
insights.locator: Those revenues are growing so quickly

insights.claim: OpenAI has shifted to net revenue, lowering its ARR from $70 billion to $50 billion, while Anthropic continues to report gross revenues and treats cloud provider payments as expenses, so reported ARR figures are not comparable.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Adjusting for gross vs net changes the apparent relative size of the two AI labs.
insights.locator: Just in the last few weeks

insights.claim: Both Anthropic and OpenAI have converged on monthly annualization, but nothing binds them to keep that convention, and Anthropic's forecast of a $100 billion-plus run rate by end-2026 opens the door to forward-revenue pricing.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Watch for convention changes in prospectus disclosures.
insights.locator: In addition, you can compute ARR

insights.claim: Analysts may shift to scaling price to revenues or earnings in 2030 or 2036, which makes multiples look lower (e.g., 25 times 2036 earnings), but investors anchored on current multiples risk mistakenly comparing forward multiples to current market multiples.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Expect bullish IPO narratives to use far-forward multiples; discount them accordingly.
insights.locator: There is a second choice that will come into play

insights.claim: Business-specific scalars such as users, eyeballs or compute power (gigawatts or compute commitments) can be used when revenue is distorted, with the logic that these lead future revenue, but they can only be computed for companies in the same business and give no sense of what is high, low or typical.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Compute-based pricing is a plausible but unanchored lens for AI lab comparison.
insights.locator: There is a third choice

insights.claim: At $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion market caps, Anthropic looks cheaper than OpenAI on latest ARR and 2026 ARR, while OpenAI is cheaper on expected 2030 revenue, compute costs and capacity, and user count; Damodaran notes both may be overpriced and comparing them just finds the less overpriced entity.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Relative-value arguments between the two labs depend entirely on metric choice; absolute valuation matters more.
insights.quote: by comparing the two, you are just finding the less overpriced entity
insights.locator: 1. Pricing metrics (table discussion)

insights.claim: Pricing difficulty depends on the number of peers and whether they are public; Anthropic and OpenAI fall into the hardest category — few companies and almost none publicly traded — because competitors like Gemini, xAI and Muse are parts of Alphabet, SpaceX and Meta respectively.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Lack of clean public comps leaves room for narrative-driven pricing and volatile post-IPO trading.
insights.locator: 2. The Peer Group challenge

insights.claim: Anthropic's IPO pricing will likely be framed first against OpenAI (public versus private), with SpaceX as a noisy peer, and then against the Mag Seven if it nears $1.5 trillion, even though Tesla, Apple and Anthropic differ greatly in business model and life-cycle stage.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Mega-cap index inclusion logic will pull Anthropic into comparison with the Magnificent Seven.
insights.locator: In the narrowest version of the pricing game

insights.claim: Bulls can argue Anthropic is cheaper than SpaceX and relatively expensive versus the Mag Seven only because of higher growth, while bears note that the AI buzz carrying Anthropic also lifts SpaceX and that the gap in revenues and earnings versus the Mag Seven cannot be explained by hope alone.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Both sides can find supporting comparables; the debate won't resolve on multiples.
insights.locator: As with the pricing comparison with OpenAI

insights.claim: Any pricing multiple connects to value through growth, reinvestment efficiency and risk: comparing PE ratios requires controlling for earnings growth, return on equity and equity risk.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Reusable checklist for judging whether a high multiple is justified.
insights.locator: 3. The Connection to Value

insights.claim: For Anthropic's EV/revenue to be justified, the determinants are revenue growth rate and speed, profitability via unit economics (gross margins) and economies of scale (compute costs growing slower than revenue), and risk from evolving business models, compute commitments and AI regulation.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Track gross margin trajectory, compute-commitment obligations and regulatory risk as the value drivers.
insights.locator: Since PE ratios are a non-starter

insights.claim: A defensible case for Anthropic at a $1.5 or $2 trillion price requires sky-high early revenue growth, operating margins surging to 30% or higher, favorable unit economics and a risk profile that converges to the average as regulatory risk recedes — a reach, but plausible.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Gives the specific bar (30%+ operating margin, rapid growth, falling risk) the market is implicitly underwriting.
insights.locator: To make a case for Anthropic at a $1.5 or $2 trillion pricing

insights.claim: The bull case rests on a massive AI addressable market, Anthropic as a big winner converting dominance into share and profit; the bear case rests on AI agent flaws, cheaper open-source competition, regulation, compute-commitment margin compression, weak governance and untrustworthy management.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Arguments built on one part of the story (growth or losses) are incomplete — like the six blind men and the elephant.
insights.locator: As Anthropic heads towards its initial public offering

insights.claim: Damodaran takes no side on Anthropic, preferring to wait for the full prospectus (hopefully next week) before doing an intrinsic valuation, as he did with SpaceX, and advises investors to step back from the frenzy.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: A widely followed valuation voice will publish a full Anthropic valuation after the S-1 — a likely sentiment catalyst.
insights.locator: I will not be taking sides here

insights.claim: A company's life-cycle stage is best read from operating metrics, not age or industry: single-digit revenue growth, stable margins and positive free cash flow mean mature, while high growth, thin or negative margins and large negative free cash flow mean young growth, regardless of scale.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Use operating metrics to avoid mislabeling aging tech companies as growth and utilities-with-data-center-demand as mature.
insights.locator: Put simply, if a company has revenue growth in single digits

insights.claim: Industry shorthand misleads: there are mature and declining companies in technology, and power companies exploiting the data center boom have become growth companies.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Utilities with data-center exposure may deserve growth framing.
insights.locator: Another choice is categorizing industry groups
